title: Primitive markings

{{Short description|Hair coloration in some equine}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2026}}
[[File:Przewalskipferd cologne.jpg|thumb|[[Przewalski's horse]] is thought to be similar in appearance to ancestors of today's domestic horses.]]

'''Primitive markings''' are a group of [[equine coat color|hair coat]] markings and qualities seen in several [[Equinae|equine]] species, including [[horse]]s, [[donkey|donkeys, and asses]].  In horses, they are associated with primitive breeds,<ref name=stachurska1999>{{Cite journal|last=Stachurska |first=AM |title=Inheritance of primitive markings in horses |journal=Journal of Animal Breeding and Genetics |year=1999 |volume=116 |pages=29–38 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0388.1999.00172.x}}</ref> though not limited to such breeds.  The markings are particularly associated with the [[Dun gene|dun]] coat color family.<ref name=ucdavis>{{Cite web|url=http://www.vgl.ucdavis.edu/services/dunhorse.php |publisher=UC Davis |access-date=2008-06-20 |title=Dun Zygosity Test}}</ref> All dun horses possess at least the [[Dorsal (anatomy)|dorsal]] stripe,<ref name=stachurska1999/><ref name=ucdavis/><ref name=lusis1943/> but the presence of the other primitive markings varies.  Other common markings may include horizontal striping on the legs, transverse striping across the shoulders, and lighter guard hairs along the edges of a dark mane and tail.<!--Summarizing all sections in lead-->

==Origin==
[[File:Lascaux2.jpg|thumb|left|alt=A cave painting of a wild horse, about 17,000 years old.|A cave painting of a wild horse, [[Lascaux]]]]
The dun coat and attendant primitive or "dun factor" markings reflect the [[wild type]] coat and are observed in all [[Equus (genus)|equine]] species.<ref name=lusis1943>{{Cite journal|last=Lusis |first=JA |title=Striping patterns in domestic horses |journal=Genetica |volume=23 |issue=1 |year=1943 |pages=31–62 |doi=10.1007/BF01763802|s2cid=19047145 }}</ref> Some cave paintings depict horses as being dun and with the primitive markings. The [[Przewalski's horse]] is dun-colored with primitive markings. So, too, are horse breeds such as the [[Konik]] and the [[Heck horse]], "bred back" to resemble the now-extinct [[tarpan]], many of which are [[grullo]] or mouse dun in color.

Every dun horse has a dorsal stripe, and some dun horses also have additional primitive markings. Some non-dun horses may also show primitive markings, namely newborn foals and horses with the non-dun 1 gene.<ref name=stachurska1999/><ref name=Imsland2015>{{cite journal | vauthors = Imsland F, McGowan K, Rubin CJ, Henegar C, Sundström E, Berglund J, Schwochow D, Gustafson U, Imsland P, Lindblad-Toh K, Lindgren G, Mikko S, Millon L, Wade C, Schubert M, Orlando L, Penedo MC, Barsh GS, Andersson L | display-authors = 6 | title = Regulatory mutations in TBX3 disrupt asymmetric hair pigmentation that underlies Dun camouflage color in horses | journal = Nature Genetics | volume = 48 | issue = 2 | pages = 152–8 | date = February 2016 | pmid = 26691985 | pmc = 4731265 | doi = 10.1038/ng.3475}}
*{{cite press release |date=December 21, 2015 |title=A horse of a different color: Genetics of camouflage and the dun pattern |website=ScienceDaily |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/12/151221133612.htm}}</ref> Primitive markings in horses are an example of [[atavism]]: preservation of or reversion to ancestral type. While primitive markings are closely linked with the dun coat colors, the variations of expression and presence in non-dun horses suggest that the markings themselves may be governed by a separate [[Genetics|genetic]] mechanism.<ref name=stachurska1999/><ref name=castle2008>{{Cite web|last=Castle |first=Nancy |title=Primitive Marking Theory |year=2008 |access-date=2008-06-20 |work=Dun Central Station |url=http://www.duncentralstation.com/PrimitiveTheory/PrimitiveMarkingTheory.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516084904/http://www.duncentralstation.com/PrimitiveTheory/PrimitiveMarkingTheory.pdf |archive-date=May 16, 2008 }}</ref>

==Dorsal stripe==
[[File:Equus kiang holdereri02.jpg|thumb|Kiangs have bold dorsal stripes.]]
Equids other than horses also exhibit a distinct dorsal stripe. Among domesticated [[donkey]]s, most have a black dorsal stripe, though it can be difficult to see on [[melanistic]] individuals.<ref name=castle2008/> In the [[African wild ass]], the dorsal stripe is thin but distinct and black. In Przewalski's horse, the dorsal stripe is usually dark brown, while it is black in the bred-back tarpan. In the [[plains zebra]], the dorsal stripe is narrow and edged by white, while in [[Grevy's zebra]], it is quite bold. The dorsal stripes of the [[onager]] and [[kiang]] are dark brown and especially vivid.

The dorsal stripe reflects the original coat color of the horse.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}} Those on bay duns may be black or reddish,<ref name=castle2008/> while those on red duns are distinctly red. Dorsal stripes on dun horses with the [[cream gene]] seem unaffected by cream: [[smoky black]]-duns ("smoky grullas"), [[buckskin (horse)|buckskin]]-duns ("dunskins"), and [[palomino]]-duns ("dunalinos") have black, brown, or red dorsal stripes, as well.

==Leg bars and markings==
[[File:Stipe-leg-pattern-on-domestic-horse-IMG 0214.jpg|right|thumb|upright|Leg bars and "zippers": This horse's legs have been shaved.]]
Also called zebra bars, tiger stripes,<ref name=ecdun>{{Cite web|url=http://www.equinecolor.com/dun.html |title=Dun |publisher=Equine Color |access-date=2008-06-20 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080525182352/http://www.equinecolor.com/dun.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = 2008-05-25}}</ref> or garters, leg bars are the most common accessory to the dorsal stripe.<ref name="stachurska1999" /> Leg bars are most commonly seen on or above the knees and [[hock (zoology)|hocks]], and reflect the underlying coat color. Leg bars on bay duns are black within the points, and reddish above them.<ref name=adultmarks>{{Cite web|url=http://www.duncentralstation.com/AdultMarkings.html |title=Adult Markings |publisher=Dun Central Station |access-date=2008-06-20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081014142256/http://www.duncentralstation.com/AdultMarkings.html |archive-date=October 14, 2008 }}</ref>

Leg bars are prominent on Grevy's zebras and mountain zebras, and African wild asses also have well-defined black leg bars below the forearm and gaskin on a white or pale background. However, as in horses, expression of leg bars seems to vary widely among donkeys, plains zebras, and Przewalski's horses, while they appear very seldom or not at all in onagers and kiangs.

Leg markings may also take the form of blotches, patches, marbling, mottling, or spotting.<ref name=stachurska1999/>

One classical genetics study concluded that stripes on the front legs seem to follow an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Inheritance of Primitive Markings in Horses | year=1999| doi=10.1111/j.1439-0388.1999.00172.x| last1=Stachurska| first1=A. M.| journal=Journal of Animal Breeding and Genetics| volume=116| pages=29–38}}</ref>

==Shoulder stripe==
[[File:Equus asinus - Ufenau 2011-07-25 17-32-24.jpg|thumb|left|Transverse shoulder stripes are common on asses.]]
The shoulder stripe is a  transverse or "vertical" marking that usually crosses the [[withers]] and extends down the shoulders.<ref name="stachurska1999" /><ref name="ecdun" /><ref name="adultmarks" />  Donkeys are known for their distinct shoulder stripe, which, when combined with the dorsal stripe, is sometimes called a "cross". It is more marked in breeds closest to the wild African ancestors of the domestic donkey.<ref name=blench>Roger Blench (2013). [http://www.soas.ac.uk/history/conferences/donkey-conference-2012/archive-of-previous-papers/file88185.pdf Wild asses and donkeys in Africa: interdisciplinary evidence for their biogeography, history and current use]. Paper presented at the School of Oriental and African Studies, London, 9 May 2012 (revised version, 2013). Accessed July 2014.</ref>  Indistinct or poorly defined markings in these regions are often called neck or shoulder smudges, patches, or shadows. Especially large markings are called neck or shoulder capes.<ref name="adultmarks" /> The kiang exhibits some shoulder smudging.

==Head markings==
[[File:Koniks5.JPG|thumb|This [[Konik]] shows the dark face mask and frosted mane common to primitive horses.]]
Many primitive markings may occur on the animal's head.
* Cobwebbing, also called spiderwebbing, consists of fine, radial stripes on the forehead.<ref name="stachurska1999" /> Among other equids, cobwebbing is most apparent in zebras.
* Face masks are areas of darker hair on the lower half of the face. These are very common.<ref name="adultmarks" />
* Ear marks are dark markings on the ears, whether the marking involves only the rim, half the back of the ear, or distinct barring or striping on the back of the ear.<ref name="adultmarks" /> These are seen almost universally throughout ''[[Equus (genus)|Equus]]''.
* Ear tips are tiny white or paler tips on the ear.<ref name="adultmarks" />
* Eye spots are found around the eyes. They are quite rare, but may be across the eye, over it, or under it.<ref name="stachurska1999" /><ref name="dungenes" />

==Guard hairs==
[[File:Fjordpferd - Kopf.jpg|thumb|right|The long-roached manes of Fjords clearly show the light, outside primitive guard hairs.]]
The dorsal stripe runs through the mane and tail of a dun horse, so the center of the mane and tail are darker. The outer edges may be significantly lighter, even close to white. These paler hairs are seen at the base of the tail and on the edges of the mane. The presence of guard hairs may also be called "frosting".<ref name="adultmarks" /> Such characteristics are very visible among the [[Fjord horse]]s, which have their sandwich-patterned manes shaved short and upright. The presence of paler guard hairs on the mane and tail is seen throughout ''[[Equus (genus)|Equus]]''.

==Other markings==
[[File:Dorsal stripe on a domestic horse IMG 0233.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Dorsal stripe and pale guard hairs on the dock of a domestic horse]]
Less common primitive markings include vertically oriented markings which may be arranged as bars, fine striping, or smudges. Such markings include:
* Dorsal barbs are suggestions of vertical striping on either side of the dorsal stripe.<ref name="stachurska1999" /><ref name="castle2008" /> They may be so closely placed that they resemble secondary dorsal stripes. Dorsal barbs are also called fishboning.<ref name=dungenes>{{Cite web |url=http://www.dungenes.org/definitions.htm |title=Definitions |publisher=Dungenes |access-date=2010-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726011032/http://www.dungenes.org/definitions.htm |archive-date=2011-07-26 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* Rib marks are extended, perhaps interrupted dorsal barbs.<ref name="castle2008" /> They are usually fine, faint stripes and may be responsible for some horses classified as [[brindle]].
* A ventral stripe runs along the midline of the underbelly of the horse. They are usually wide and are uncommon.<ref name="adultmarks" />
* Zippers are lines of paler hairs running vertically along the back of the animal's leg, usually from the hoof to the knee.<ref name=grulladcs>{{Cite web|url=http://www.duncentralstation.com/Grulla.html |title=Grulla |publisher=Dun Central Station |access-date=2008-06-26 |quote="Zippers" on the backs of the fetlocks of dun dilute colored horses is a common sight. When clipped, the light line running up the back of the fetlock will be very crisp. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080411015711/http://www.duncentralstation.com/Grulla.html |archive-date=April 11, 2008 }}</ref> Because they consist of paler hairs and are found where horses often have feathering, zippers are considered by some to be guard hairs.
* Bider markings are only known in Przewalski's horses and native [[Mongolian horse]]s from nearby. The bider is mostly symmetrical and found near the front of each shoulder, near the chest. The size of the bider ranges from a small dark spot to a large, webbed cape of darker skin and hair.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jes/18/4/18_4_145/_article|title=New Primitive Marking (Bider) in Mongolian Native Horse and Equus przewalskii|author1=Mioko MASUDA|author2=Junko TSUNODA|author3=Hiroko NOMURA|author4=Nami KIMURA|author5=Gombojav ALTANGEREL|author6=Bandi NAMKHAI|author7=Usukhjargal DOLJ|author8=Michinari YOKOHAMA|journal=Journal of Equine Science|volume=18|year=2007|issue=4|pages=145–151|doi=10.1294/jes.18.145|access-date=2008-12-19|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Primitive markings in non-dun horses==
[[File: Countershading stripe.jpg|thumb| This horse's dorsal stripe is most likely caused by non-dun 1.]]
Less distinct primitive markings can also occur on non-dun horses, even in breeds which are not known to have any dun individuals. The most common primitive marking found is a dorsal stripe.<ref name=stachurska1999/>  Most non-dun horses do not have darker primitive markings, but some do. This is because there are two types of non-dun, called ''non-dun1'' and ''non-dun2''. Non-dun 1 removes the diluting effect of dun, but keeps the primitive markings, while non-dun 2 removes both the diluting effect and the primitive markings.<ref name=etalon>{{cite web |url=https://www.etalondx.com/dun#! |title=More about Dun and Primitive Markings |publisher=Etalon Diagnostics |access-date=2019-04-28}}</ref> The ''non-dun1'' allele is over 40,000 years old, while ''non-dun2'' is relatively recent, and is thought to have first appeared within the past several thousand years.<ref name=Imsland2015/> Primitive markings on non-duns can be seasonal, visible only when the horse is shedding its coat.<ref name=lookalikecollage>{{Cite web|url=http://www.duncentralstation.com/Look-A-LikeCollages.html |title=Look-A-Like Collages |work=Dun Look-A-Likes |publisher=Dun Central Station |author=Nancy Castle |access-date=2008-06-26 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081012141250/http://www.duncentralstation.com/Look-A-LikeCollages.html |archive-date=October 12, 2008 }}</ref>

Dorsal stripes and other primitive markings on non-dun horses used to be called "countershading" dorsals<ref name=castle2008/> before their genetic cause was discovered at the ''dun'' locus.<ref name=Imsland2015/> This is not to be confused with the camouflage mechanism of [[countershading]].

===Primitive markings in foals===
Many [[foal]]s, particularly if they are [[buckskin (horse)|buckskin]], [[smoky black]], or [[black (horse)|black]], are born with primitive markings such as dorsal stripes and leg bars that disappear after the foal coat sheds. Such horses are sometimes mistakenly registered as dun. This error seems particularly common in foals that turn [[Gray (horse)|gray]].<ref name=castle2008/><!--is this bit on gray what the source says?  Odd, as more often I've seen gray foals that are the opposite--they have no dorsal striping (OK to delete this once read-->
